Name: Leptis Magna, Coastal Bastion of Eastern North Africa: The Saharan Trade Route
RagShortTexts: Leptis Magna holds a deep-water harbor on the Gulf of Greater Syrtis that leads straight into the depths of the Sahara
It monopolizes the export of gold, ivory and rare beasts from inner Africa and is an important source of Carthage's foreign trade revenue
Secure in the southeast, it read the course of the Punic wars shrewdly and preserved its merchants' autonomous privileges
BaseText: Leptis Magna (town_carthage_lepqi, near modern Khoms in Libya) lies on the western shore of the Gulf of Greater Syrtis, and it is the eastern trading gateway founded by the Phoenicians in the seventh century BC. The city sits on a natural harbor at the mouth of the Wadi Lebda, backed by vast wastelands, and is the most important terminus where the trans-Saharan camel caravans crossing the desert reach the Mediterranean. A steady stream of gold, ivory and ebony from inner Africa, together with the fierce North African leopards and elephants that the gladiatorial arenas badly needed, was all shipped out from here. Because it lay far from the main battlefields in Italy and Iberia, Leptis Magna kept up a relatively peaceful prosperity during the Second Punic War, paid its war taxes to Carthage on schedule, and at the end of the war shrewdly went over to the victor to preserve the city's autonomous trading rights.

Variants.Content: The docks of Leptis Magna always carry the scent of exotic spices. Whether war rages or peace returns, the gold caravans of the Sahara never stop.
This rich harbor on a distant eastern sea has shown Rome the endless treasures of inner Africa. The Senate is glad to accept its tribute and goodwill.
We cross the long, scorching desert to bring ivory to Leptis Magna, and the white-robed Phoenicians gild it, but the storms deep in the desert have never belonged to any king.
